_comment: Declared policy for what the dotnet feedstock tracks. Human-owned: the
automation reads this and never edits it. Everything the bot cannot decide
for itself is decided here, or escalated as a GitHub issue.
Why this file exists: the workflow used to hardcode `channel: ['10.0']` in a
matrix, which meant .NET 11 and 12 would ship and the bot would stay silent
forever while still reporting success. Blindness that looks like health.
A conda-forge feedstock publishes ONE `dotnet` package, so tracking a new
release line means leaving the old one. That is a judgment call about what
users of a scientific packaging channel want, not something metadata can
answer -- hence `policy` below, and hence new lines become issues, not PRs.
_tracked_comment: Release line -> the upstream feedstock branch that ships it.
This feedstock maintains several lines at once. Upstream branches are
main v2 v3 v5 v6 v7 v8: when a new line takes over `main`, the previous one
gets a `vN` branch so it can keep receiving patches. conda-forge accumulates
every published version, so users can pin `dotnet=8`.
Each tracked line is planned and bumped independently against its own
branch, so concurrent bumps never conflict.
EOL lines (v3, v5, v6, v7) are deliberately absent: they sit at their
final released versions and Microsoft will publish no more, so there is
nothing to detect and watching them would only add noise.
_policy_comment: latest - any line that leaves preview (reaches GA), LTS or STS alike.
lts    - only Long Term Support lines. LTS is 3 years of support and lands
on even majors (8, 10, 12); STS is 18 months, odd majors
(7, 9, 11). Both reach GA the same way -- the difference is only
manual - never adopt; only bump what is already in `tracked`.
`latest` is set because it matches what this feedstock has always done:
conda-forge published 7.0.410 and 9.0.203, both STS lines, and each held
`main` in its turn (upstream still has the v7 branch from when 7.0 handed
over). Following every release is cheap here precisely because several lines
are maintained at once -- moving `main` to 11.0 does not take 10.0 away,
since v10 keeps receiving patches and users can pin `dotnet=10`.
Separately, and regardless of policy: a line still supported (active or
maintenance) but absent from `tracked` is escalated as a maintenance gap.
9.0 is exactly that today -- published as 9.0.203 from main, then 10.0
replaced it and no v9 branch was ever cut, so it sits orphaned nine patch
releases behind with nowhere to patch from. Automating the transition below
_transition_comment: When a newer line reaches GA, the convention is: cut a vN branch from
`main` so the outgoing line stays patchable, then move `main` to the new
line. Verified mechanical -- rendering the recipe at 11.0.100 needs no edits
beyond the two version variables, because `framework` derives net11.0 and
cut_branch_upstream: create the vN ref directly on the upstream feedstock.
This is the one action not mediated by a PR, because a ref cannot be created
by one. It is non-destructive -- a new ref only, never a force-update, and
the job aborts if the branch already exists. Set false to have the branch
pushed to the fork instead, leaving you one `git push upstream vN` to run.
_issue_repo_comment: Where judgment-call issues get filed. Defaults to this repo rather than the
feedstock so an unattended bot does not post into a shared conda-forge repo.
Point it at conda-forge/dotnet-feedstock if you would rather co-maintainers
see them -- the token needs issues:write there if you do.
_abi_comment: Check the ABI Microsoft's artifacts REQUIRE against what the recipe
DECLARES, per Linux platform, on every run. See scripts/abi_probe.py.
This exists because the bot was blind to a whole class of drift. It knew
two version-coupled facts -- sdk_version and runtime_version -- and
verified one integrity fact, the sha256. The ABI floor is a third, and it
had already moved without anyone noticing:
glibc:   .NET 8 and 9 need 2.17; .NET 10 raised it to 2.27. The recipe
declared 2.17 for the whole 10.0 line, so conda-forge published
packages advertising `__glibc >=2.17` that cannot load below
2.27. They install, then fail at first use.
openssl: the crypto shim dlopens a fixed soname list, topping out at
libssl.so.3 through .NET 10 -- hence the `openssl <4` pin, since
openssl 4.x ships only libssl.so.4. .NET 11 preview.6 adds
libssl.so.4, so that pin goes stale in the other direction the
moment 11 ships.
Both drifts happened at a MAJOR boundary, which is where this bot already
escalates to a human -- so this adds an assertion at an existing gate
rather than new machinery. It is still checked every run, because sampling
only the newest patch of each line cannot prove a patch release never
moves a floor.
Findings are always escalated, never auto-fixed. Raising c_stdlib_version
drops users below the new floor and changing an openssl pin changes what
resolves for everyone; neither is mechanical.
Cost is one ~30 MB runtime tarball per tracked line per Linux platform.
The runtime tarball rather than the SDK's ~240 MB because all the native
code lives there -- the aspnetcore framework and the sdk tree ship zero
.so files. Set enabled false to skip it.
_rid_map_comment: Microsoft RID -> conda-forge subdir. Used to audit which architectures
Microsoft offers against which the recipe actually packages. The set the
recipe packages is NOT duplicated here; it is read from PLATFORMS in
update-dotnet-version.py so the two cannot drift.
A RID mapped here is *mappable*, not necessarily *viable* -- see
_ignore_rids_comment: RIDs with no usable conda-forge equivalent. conda-forge has no musl subdir,
so those can never be packaged and should not generate recurring noise.
_active_subdirs_comment: conda-forge subdirs that are actively built. This is the PRIMARY viability
gate and it is declared, not inferred, because inference got it wrong:
The repodata-size heuristic alone passed win-32 (10.4 MB, 24,464 packages),
but conda-forge stopped building win-32 in 2019 -- newest package there is
dated 2019-02-20. Size distinguishes 'has an ecosystem' from 'empty', but
not 'thriving' from 'frozen and abandoned'. Detecting that from timestamps
would mean downloading repodata (432 MB for linux-64), which CI cannot do.
So: a subdir must be listed here AND pass min_repodata_bytes. Keep this in
sync with what conda-forge actually builds.
_viability_comment: A conda-forge subdir existing is not the same as it being usable. Learned
the hard way on issue #115: linux-armv7l is a real subdir whose repodata is
1,306 bytes -- 3 packages, no icu/openssl/zlib -- so a dotnet built there
would install and be unusable. win-arm64's repodata is ~777 KB (1,927
repodata.json Content-Length is a deliberately cheap proxy for ecosystem
size: one HEAD request, no download. linux-64's repodata is ~432 MB, so
actually fetching these to count packages is not an option in CI.
It is a heuristic, not a guarantee.
